summary: Objects to the requirement that hosts implement the Telnet Go-Ahead command. The author calls it unappealing, says it will not serve its purpose unless hosts make unwarranted assumptions, and raises a third line of objections.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 596 argues that Telnet's Go-Ahead signal should not be required. The author says it can arrive at the wrong time, cause a deadlock and be difficult to support across different host systems.

subtitle: An argument against requiring Telnet's Go-Ahead command on every host.

tldr.problem: The Telnet specification requires the Go-Ahead command, but Taft argues that it is often unnecessary, can fail to work as intended, and is difficult for many hosts to implement correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives a deadlock example and lists problems caused by different ways hosts handle terminal input, output and processes.
tldr.outcome: The author proposes removing Go-Ahead or making it a negotiated option that is suppressed by default.

today: The unit records RFC 596's status as Unknown and lists no updates or obsoleting RFCs. It argues that Go-Ahead should be removed or negotiated with suppression as the default.

sections.title: What the Go-Ahead Command Does
sections.content:
Taft objects to requiring hosts to implement Telnet's Go-Ahead (GA) command. He says GA is unattractive, may not serve its purpose without assumptions about other hosts, and is impossible for many hosts to implement correctly in all cases.

The RFC defines half-duplex as communication that can proceed in only one direction at a time; the receiver must wait until the sender gives up control. It distinguishes this from the use of “half-duplex” to mean remote rather than local character echoing.
sections.plainLanguage: Go-Ahead is meant to signal a change in who may use a half-duplex communication path. The author argues that a universal requirement for it does not fit how many hosts work.

sections.title: Why the Default Should Suppress GA
sections.content:
The Telnet specification assumes half-duplex, line-at-a-time communication as normal. Taft argues that interactive systems are moving away from that model and that only a minority of terminals need GA. He says the default should favor the option state most hosts are willing to use.

He also argues that keeping GA enabled by default would increase network traffic for character-at-a-time input. In his view, parties that do not need the mechanism should not have to negotiate its suppression.
sections.plainLanguage: The author says most terminals do not need GA. He therefore wants it switched off by default, rather than making every host negotiate to turn it off.

sections.title: How an Early GA Can Cause Deadlock
sections.content:
The RFC describes a user who types a line that the user's network software splits into multiple messages. The server process receives the first part, waits for more input, and the server Telnet sends GA before the rest arrives.

That GA can unlock the user's keyboard while output from the computer is blocked. The user and computer then wait on each other until the user manually gives control back. Taft says the server cannot generally know exactly when the user host has reached the end of a line, so restricting GA to that condition does not solve the general problem.
sections.plainLanguage: If GA arrives before the full line reaches the server, the user's terminal may start accepting input while blocking computer output. Both sides can then wait until the user intervenes.

sections.title: Different Hosts Behave Differently
sections.content:
Some host processes do not block while waiting for terminal input; they poll or accept input through interrupts. In those cases, the server Telnet may never send GA even when the process can accept input. A host may also have more than one process sharing a terminal, so one process can wait for input while another produces output.

Inter-terminal links can connect multiple terminals and processes, and system messages may need to reach a terminal asynchronously. Taft argues that these arrangements do not fit the GA mechanism's assumptions. He proposes either removing GA or making it a negotiated option suppressed by default.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts may share terminals among processes, poll for input or send system notices at any time. The author says these differences make a single GA rule unreliable.
